# The data

The same file as in Ex-8-1, `data/8-1-county-crops.csv`: one row per county and year, Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska, 2000 to 2018. `corn_yield` is in bushels per acre; `weeks_extreme` is the number of weeks from May to September in extreme or exceptional drought (US Drought Monitor categories D3 and D4). A county-year **with extreme drought** has `weeks_extreme` of 1 or more.

# Task 1: Predict, no AI

The table in this worksheet has one row per state, with: the average corn yield without extreme drought, the average with it, the difference, and the **share of county-years with extreme drought, in percent**.

**A. Colorado has 154 county-years, and 43 of them have extreme drought. What share, in percent, must the table show for Colorado? Compute it by hand.**

Your answer:

**B. In which unit will you ask the AI to compute the share: as a share between 0 and 1, or as a percentage between 0 and 100? Either is fine; write down which, because the format the AI picks has to match it.**

# Task 2: The table, in gt

**My request to the AI.** Fill in every `<...>`:

```text
In my R project, data/8-1-county-crops.csv has one row per county and
year, with corn_yield (bushels per acre) and weeks_extreme (weeks from
May to September in extreme or exceptional drought). A county-year with
extreme drought has weeks_extreme of 1 or more.

The message: in all three states, corn yields were lower in county-years
with extreme drought, which hit about a quarter of county-years. The
reader: <...>.

Make a finished table with one row per state, ordered by <...>, with the
columns: state; average corn yield without extreme drought; average
with extreme drought; the difference; and the share of county-years
with extreme drought in percent, computed as <...>. Use gt. Check that
the table has 3 rows, and that the share for Colorado shows as <...>%,
which I computed myself. Build every number in the notes that depends
on the drought threshold (such as "at least 1 week") from the same
threshold the code uses, not as typed text.

Every table must meet this standard:
1. Column headers and row labels in plain words with units, such as
   "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name such as
   corn_yield.
2. Categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
3. Numbers rounded to what the message needs, with the same number of
   decimals down each column.
4. Thousands separators in large numbers, except in years.
5. Percentages shown as percentages.
6. Numbers right-aligned so that the digits line up; text left-aligned.
7. Text no smaller than the document's body text.
8. Fits the page width where it will appear, without scrolling.
9. Rows in an order that serves the message (by value, or in time
   order), not alphabetical unless the reader will search a long table.
10. A title that says what the numbers are.
11. A note giving the source of the data.
12. A note saying how any computed column was computed.
13. The number of observations behind each value, when it varies.
14. Nothing the message does not need: no extra columns, no row
    numbers, no heavy borders, no colours that only decorate.
For regression tables, also:
15. One column per model, with headers or a title saying what each
    model explains.
16. Standard errors in parentheses below each estimate, with their kind
    stated in a note.
17. Significance stars left out, or defined in a note and used the same
    way in every table.
18. The number of observations for every model.
```
